body.text: New Zealand's incumbent government fails to secure majority from election result
In short:
New Zealand's Electoral Commission has released the results from the country's national election held on November 7.
The incumbent government, led by the National Party's Christopher Luxon, fell short of a ruling majority by a single seat.
What's next?
If Mr Luxon fails to negotiate a deal to form government with the Opportunity party, the country may have to have another election.
New Zealand's incumbent Prime Minister Christopher Luxon will need to secure support from the centrist Opportunity party if he wants to form a new government.
Preliminary results from the New Zealand election on November 7 had Mr Luxon's current three-party ruling coalition holding a slim majority of two seats.

But the final election results just released by New Zealand's Electoral Commission — which include roughly 400,000 special votes counted over the past three weeks — show the Coalition has secured 65 seats, one short of a majority.
That means Mr Luxon will need to negotiate with Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong to secure power once again.
Luxon's centre-right National Party secured 40 seats, against 36 seats for the main centre-left opposition Labour.
The data shows a centre-left coalition of Labour, the Green Party and Te Pati Maori would not be able to form a government, even with Opportunity's support.
However, if NZ First was to strike a deal with the centre-left parties, as it did with Labour after the 2017 election, it could form a coalition government.

If Mr Luxon cannot reach either a coalition or confidence-and-supply deal, and any negotiations between other parties fail to produce a majority government, New Zealand will have to hold fresh elections.
"New Zealanders need a government that is stable, that works together and will last for the full term," he told a news conference.
"Kiwis won't thank us for rushing to an agreement that falls apart or for sending them back to the polls."
During the election campaign, Mr Luxon repeatedly ruled out working with Opportunity.
However, he said he had heard from constituents during the campaign that they wanted their leaders "to find common ground and to get on with delivering for them".
"I've heard the message, and I'll be taking that into these negotiations," he said.
"Over the past few weeks, I have spoken with Winston [Peters] and David [Seymour] and Qiulae [Wong], and with the final result now known, formal negotiations will begin."
The final tally considers special votes, which include those from overseas voters or people outside their electorate and which typically skew left.
According to the Electoral Commission, three seats have shifted since the election-night preliminary count.
The National Party has lost two since then while the Green Party has 17 seats — its best ever result — compared with 16 on election night.
ACT New Zealand has 13 seats, New Zealand First Party 12 seats, Opportunity Party seven seats and Te Pāti Māori five seats.

"There is an overhang of 10 seats because the National Party won six more electorate seats than it would otherwise have from its share of the party vote and Te Pāti Māori won four more electorate seats," the authority said in a statement.
The commission says the body is prepared for another election if one is called.
"We always need to be ready for another election, so we would be prepared if another one was called," chief electoral officer Karl Le Quesne told RNZ.
'It's not just up to us'
Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong told reporters in New Zealand that she was preparing to begin negotiations with Mr Luxon and his National Party.
When she was asked if voters could be forced back to the polls if they could not strike a deal, Ms Wong said it was "really important to remember there are seven parties in parliament".
"Everyone is responsible for making sure we do everything we can to deliver a state of government," she said.
"It's not just up to us."

Ms Wong has previously declared that she would not back the existing coalition if Winston Peters remained as foreign minister. She told journalists that was still a requirement for her party to give support.

She also pointed back to the "bottom lines" she unveiled earlier this year, reiterating that a coalition would have to regulate lobbying, tackle uncompetitive behaviour in the supermarket sector, develop a new plan for the health sector and recommit to the Paris Agreement on climate change if it wanted to secure her support.
"Our bottom lines are the minimum non-negotiables we require for a confidence in supply or a coalition deal," she said.
She also said that Opportunity could remain on the crossbench while ensuring the government retained confidence in supply.
"All options are on the table," she said.
At a press conference, Labour leader Chris Hipkins pointed out his party had won the popular vote but acknowledged that did not guarantee a route to government.
"As to my own future, that's something that I'll make further decisions on once it's clear a new government has been formed and we've had a chance to regroup as the Labour team."
ABC/Reuters
